newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: JCI, Shell deal to underpin mooted listing.
newsitem.headline: JCI, Shell deal to underpin mooted listing.

text.p: JCI Ltd's planned purchase of Shell South Africa's coal interests signalled its emergence as a key player in the coal export industry which would underpin its mooted stock market listing, analysts said on Tuesday.

Shell International Ltd announced on Tuesday that it had signed a letter of intent to sell its 50 percent share in the Rietspruit joint venture with Ingwe Coal Corp, a 6.82 percent share in the Richards Bay Coal Terminal Company (RBCT) and some 2.1 billion tons of coal reserves.
Analysts felt the most significant feature in the deal was JCI's purchase of the RBCT stake.

"The 6.82 pct of RBCT is the most important bit in it because what it does is give JCI the chance for expansion," said Societe Generale Frankel Pollak analyst Ross Gardner. "It gives them some growth potential which they would need to go and list."
Analysts say the company plans to list its coal interests separately, although the timing is unclear at this stage.

"Allocation to the harbour is highly sought after and Shell's quota is normally quoted on the market, in other words they bargain for it on an ad hoc basis," said another analyst who asked not to be named.
"And with JCI picking it up it takes allocation out of the market. It places additional value on it first of all and secondly enhances JCI's position as a major exporter of coal," the analyst said.
Gardner also noted that the purchase of the allocation could put the squeeze on Duiker Mining Ltd and Anglovaal Minerals.
"Duiker and Anglovaal Minerals export more than their allocation so therefore they buy allocations from other people," he said.

"With Sasol joining RBCT and now the Shell allocation being taken up by JCI, it cuts down the possibility for buying of allocations from people. It restricts Duiker's mining plans and Avmin's expansion plans," he said.
Analysts said that the bulk of the purchase price, rumoured to be between 400 and 500 million rand, appeared to be primarily for the RBCT stake.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell analyst John Loewen said he was concerned that if the price proved to be correct, it might be on the high side.
"If the rumour is correct that it is 400 to 500 million, looking at my valuations for the Shell assets I would be concerned that they would be at the top end of the range," Loewen said.
Analysts said despite the fact that Rietspruit's life span would come to an end at the end of the century, its acquisition by JCI could hold other benefits.
"The first is its washing plant and loading terminal which are very good for JCI's expansion plans," Gardner said. "The second one is because (JCI's) Tavistock colliery is contiguous to Rietspruit."
Analysts said that while Ingwe has a pre-emptive right on the Rietspruit stake, they were unlikely to exercise that option, allowing JCI to develop synergies between the two collieries.
"The only way Rietspruit could extend its life was to work with Tavistock so it is a very good move," said Simpson McKie James Capel analyst Albert Monissian.
JCI shares were trading 50 cents higher at 44.50 rand on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange at noon on Tuesday.
